newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Rise in German unemployment slows in February.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Rise in German unemployment slows in February.

text.p: German unemployment worsened again in February but the rise in joblessness slowed, the Federal Labour Office said on Thursday, prompting analysts to predict the worst of the jobs crisis may be over.

Still, unemployment remains at the highest levels since the great depression of the 1930s, undermining German efforts to cut its budget deficit and eroding what leverage it has to exclude supposedly weaker nations from European monetary union (EMU), slated to start in January 1999, economists said.

Unemployment rose a mere 5,000 to a seasonally adjusted 4.316 million in February, the Federal Labour Office said. The Bundesbank said the unemployment rate was unchanged from January at 11.3 percent.
The unadjusted total number of unemployed was 4.672 million, up from 4.658 million in January. The unadjusted rate was also unchanged at 12.2 percent.

In January, a sharp rise of 145,000 in the seasonally adjusted total fuelled speculation Germany would fail to narrow its budget gap this year and miss the deficit target for the single European currency.

Labour Office President Bernhard Jagoda told a news conference the worst of Germany's jobs crisis may now be over since the rise in unemployment slowed sharply in February. He added he expected a decline in unemployment in March.

"In non-construction related manufacturing areas, the rise in unemployment was noticeably smaller than overall. This could mean that the worst is over in job losses in the manufacturing industry," Jagoda said.
But he added that the construction sector remained very weak in February, and that the economy provided no stimulus for jobs creation.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel said late on Wednesday that Germany must achieve a labour market turnaround by summer to meet the Maastricht convergence criteria.
Uwe Angenendt of BHF-Bank said the February data confirmed his estimation that the rise in unemployment was caused by special factors in January such as cold weather.
But he added he has raised his estimation of Germany's 1997 budget deficit to 3.3 percent of gross domestic product from three percent.
High unemployment makes it harder for Germany to cut its budget deficit because it diminishes tax revenue and increases spending for jobless benefits.
Countries hoping to participate in EMU should have budget deficits of three percent of GDP or below. The decision on who will participate in EMU at the start will be based on 1997 economic data.
While the Maastricht Treaty allows some leeway in meeting the targets, Germany has been one of the strongest opponents of a loose interpretation.

Many analysts see this as an effort to exclude southern European countries such as Italy, Spain and Portugal from EMU because their spotty track record as inflation fighters could weaken the future single currency.

Germany's participation in EMU is seen as indispensible to the success of the project. But if it misses the targets, it would have a weaker position to bar others that in the past few years have travelled farther down the convergence road.
"Germany's bargaining position for keeping Italy out of EMU is weakened," said Joerg Kraemer at Merrill Lynch. "Therefore there will be broad EMU rather than core EMU."
Huw Roberts of Natwest agreed. "The labour market remains extremely weak as far as we can tell. ... That means that others will be able to extract a greater compromise in EMU negotiations."
Market reaction to the data was limited. German bonds fell from earlier highs in response to the better than expected figure. The German DAX, buoyed by a strong dollar, was at near-record levels.
In west Germany, the adjusted number of unemployed fell by 4,000 to 3.018 million in February. The unemployment rate was unchanged at 10.6 percent.
In east Germany, the adjusted number of unemployed rose by 9,000 to 1.298 million. The unemployment rate was 18.9 percent, up from 18.7 percent.
-- Bonn newsroom, 49-228-2609750
